title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Preface: How to Use This Book
Change one number in a dataset, and how many documents are now wrong? If the number was copied by hand into a report, a slide, an email and a web page, nobody knows without searching. This book teaches a way of publishing with nothing to search for: you write once, in plain text, and a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an e-book, a website, a blog and a dashboard all rebuild from that one source with one command. The program that rebuilds them is Quarto.
crumbs: Preface: How to Use This Book

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Prompt, Check, Publish
The title names the method, a loop you run at every step of both projects. You prompt a coding assistant, a program that writes files and runs commands at your request, describing one small piece of work with its files and columns named. You check what it did: read what changed, look at the result, compare it with the data. An assistant can be fluent, fast and wrong, so this step is never skipped, and it is always yours. Then Quarto publishes, rebuilding every output from the checked source the same way every time. Chapter 1 explains why the last step can be trusted, and Chapter 2 how to make the first two reliable.

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Who this book is for
I wrote this book for researchers, practitioners, lecturers and students: anyone who works with data and needs to share the results. It shows how to publish from one source of text, code and data, using Quarto, which is free and open source, so every report, slide deck and web page is reproducible, interactive and of publication quality. With a coding assistant, work that once took days now takes minutes. Along the way, I explain the concepts, arguments and decisions behind each step.
You may be new to Quarto, to coding assistants or to both. No programming is assumed: I explain the Python the assistant writes, but you do not have to write it. If the terminal is new to you, Chapter 3 teaches the little you need, one checked step at a time.
You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free GitHub account, and an account with one coding assistant (Before you start lists what each needs).

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
The two running examples
Every concept is tied to one of two projects, both built on real, cited data.
A London visitor guide (Part II). For the city’s tourism office, you write one guide that becomes a web page, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for managers and a published website. Every visitor number in it, from the 7,116,929 visits to the Natural History Museum (South Kensington) in 2025 down, is computed from the counts published by the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions.
Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities (Part III). You group Colombia’s municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, from 2016 to 2023, compare health and education outcomes between the kinds, and publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all from one analysis script. Most of the data are Colombian open data, joined by official municipality codes; rainfall comes from CHIRPS and altitude from NASA’s SRTM (Appendix G — Data Sources, Licences and Credits).

When you get stuck
You will get stuck: an install fails, a prompt goes wrong, a render stops with an error you have never seen. That is expected, and the book is built for it. Every hands-on block ends at a checkpoint, a folder in the workshop repository (checkpoints/) holding the project as it should be at that point, with a README listing the steps to catch up. The rule is simple: stuck for two minutes, catch up, and rejoin at the next block. Each exercise ends with its catch-up line, which you paste into your assistant (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.



A checkpoint holds the end of its block, so it can be ahead of the step you were on: after catching up, skip the block’s remaining prompts and read on to the next exercise. Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers lists every checkpoint.

text:
Three chapters stand between you and the first project: one for the Publish step of the loop, one for Prompt and Check, and one for the machine that runs them all.
Chapter 1, Publishing That Rebuilds Itself. Why hand-made reports drift out of date, and how Quarto rebuilds every output from one source so that they cannot. title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.1 Why reports drift
Most reports are built by hand. An analyst runs a script, copies a number into a Word document, pastes a chart into a slide, retypes the same number in an email, and exports a PDF for the website. Every copy is a small act of faith that the number was right and is still right. When the data change, someone has to find every copy, and nobody can say for sure where each one came from.
The alternative is one source that rebuilds every output, the Publish step of this book’s loop. By the end of this chapter you will be able to say, for any document Quarto builds, where each number came from and what happens to every copy when it changes. You will also know when the whole approach is not worth it.
The London visitor guide that runs through Part II is a small example of a common problem. The tourism office publishes the same facts to several audiences: a web guide for visitors, a dashboard for managers, a Word brief for partners, a square social-media card and, later, a white paper. In the finished project, five pages read the same table of attraction visits, and between them they write ten files: the guide alone becomes a web page, a Word document, a PDF, a PowerPoint deck, an e-book and a set of slides.
Suppose the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions (ALVA), the source of those counts, corrects one figure. In a copy-and-paste workflow, that correction has to reach ten files by hand. Three things tend to go wrong:
None of these is a failure of care. They are what happens when the output is treated as the thing you edit. The fix is structural: edit the source, and let a program rebuild the outputs.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.2 What Quarto is
Quarto is an open-source publishing system: a command-line program, free for anyone to use, that turns plain-text source files into finished documents.
The input is either a plain Markdown file (.md) or a Quarto document (.qmd). A .qmd file is Markdown with two additions: a block of settings at the top, written in YAML, and code cells, fenced blocks of code that run when the document is built. Here is a complete one, the file the test run in Chapter 3 asks your assistant to write:
---
title: "Hello"
format:
  html: default
  typst: default
---

```{python}
answer = 6 * 7
```

The answer is `{python} answer`.
The sentence at the bottom contains inline code: when the document is built, Quarto runs answer and writes its value into the sentence. When this book was built, the same calculation gave 42, and that number was computed, not typed.

1.2.1 Three steps: execute, convert, typeset
quarto render does three things in order (Figure 1.1).






Figure 1.1: What quarto render does. One source becomes Markdown with results, which Pandoc converts to each output format; for PDF, Typst typesets the result.




Execute. A computation engine runs the code cells: Jupyter for Python, knitr for R. The results (numbers, tables, figures) replace the code in an intermediate Markdown file. The cells run once for each format, so each output gets results made for it (Section 5.4). This book uses Python only.
Convert. For each format, Pandoc, a long-established document converter, reads that Markdown and writes the output: HTML, Word (docx), EPUB, PowerPoint (pptx) or a Reveal.js slide deck.
Typeset. For PDF, Pandoc writes source for Typst, a modern typesetting system that ships inside Quarto, and Typst produces the PDF. No LaTeX installation is needed. (Quarto can also make PDFs through LaTeX, format: pdf, if you install a TeX distribution.)

The split matters in practice. A failure in step 1 is a failure of your code: a missing package, a wrong column name, a cell that raises an error. A failure in step 2 or 3 is a failure of the document: a malformed table, an image too large for the page, a format-specific option that does not exist. When a render fails, the error message tells you which step stopped, and that tells you where to look.






NoteWhy this works



Pandoc converts between many formats by reading every input into one internal document model and writing every output from that model. That is why one Markdown file can become both a Word document and a slide deck: neither output is derived from the other. Both come from the same kind of structured intermediate, built from the same source, so a heading is a heading everywhere.

text:
1.3 Quarto is not AI
This book pairs Quarto with a coding assistant, and the pairing invites a misunderstanding: that Quarto itself is an AI tool. It is not. Quarto is conventional software. Given the same source files and the same data, it writes the same outputs every time. It does not generate text, code or figures of its own, and it sends nothing to an AI service.
The assistant is a separate program. It reads and writes the files in your project folder and runs commands you approve; Quarto then turns those files into formats. The two have different failure modes, and the workflow in this book is designed around the difference:



Table 1.2: Two tools with different failure modes.

Quarto

Because generation and rendering are separate, every mistake the assistant makes lands in a file you can read or a command you approve before anything is published: that gap is where the Check step of the loop happens. And because the render is repeatable, anyone can rebuild your outputs to confirm them, without trusting the assistant at all.






WarningCommon pitfall



Quarto runs whatever code your cells contain. If a cell calls an AI service, the document becomes as unpredictable as that service, and the cause is your code, not Quarto. Keep calls to models out of rendered documents unless the variation is the point.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.4 Reproducible: same source, same result
Reproducible is used loosely, so here is the precise sense this book means: someone else, or you in six months, can rebuild the same results from the same files with one command, and can see where every number came from. Four properties make that possible:
One source. Text, code and data live in plain files in one folder. Nothing important exists only inside an application.
Numbers are computed. Every figure, table and number in a sentence comes from a code cell or inline code that reads the data. Nothing is typed in or pasted from elsewhere.
One command. quarto render rebuilds everything. There is no sequence of manual export steps to remember.
Versioned. Git, the version-control tool installed in Chapter 3, is something like Word’s Track Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history. Each state of the source, data and settings that you choose to record becomes a commit, with a message saying why it changed. Any earlier state can be restored, two states can be compared, and a result can be tied to the exact files that made it. The project’s Python packages are pinned too, in a lockfile (uv.lock, introduced in Chapter 4), so a colleague’s machine builds the same environment as yours.
Together these turn the drift problem around. Correct one value in the data, render, and the table, the chart and the sentence that quote it all update together, in every format.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. You correct one number in the data. What do you retype in the report?
Nothing. You fix the data file and render again. If the answer is anything else, some number in the report was typed rather than computed, and that is the bug to fix.








WarningCommon pitfall



Reproducible does not mean correct. A wrong analysis reproduces perfectly: the same wrong number appears in every format, every time. Reproducibility makes errors findable, because anyone can trace a number back to its code and data, but you still have to check results against their sources. Chapter 13 is an extended example of a result that reproduces cleanly and still must not be read the way it first appears.


There is one more subtlety, which matters once projects grow. Rendering every page from scratch can be slow, so Quarto can cache results with a setting called freeze. A cache is only as good as its rule for throwing results away, and Quarto re-executes a frozen page when that page’s source changes, not when a data file it reads changes. Chapter 14 shows how to use the cache safely. This book itself uses one, with a documented way to clear it (Appendix H).

text:
1.5 When Quarto is the wrong tool
Quarto earns its keep when the same content is rebuilt, either because the data change or because the content goes to several audiences. It costs you a plain-text workflow, a command line and some setup. That trade is not always worth making:

Collaborators who edit in Word. If the people who revise the document work in a word processor with tracked changes, they can comment on the Word output, but their edits have to be carried back into the source by hand. For documents whose main work is multi-author line editing, a shared word processor may simply fit better.
Designed layouts. Quarto produces structured documents: headings, paragraphs, figures, tables. Typst and CSS can take the look a long way, but a poster or a brand-heavy brochure laid out to the millimetre is easier in a design tool.
Format fidelity at the edges. Each format can only carry what it supports. Pandoc writes good Word and PowerPoint files, but a PowerPoint table cannot hold pictures, for example, so the London guide’s photo table shows each photo’s alt text in its pptx version instead. Check every format you promise to deliver.
One-off documents. A two-paragraph note with no data and no second audience gains little from a build system.







TipIn practice



A useful test: will this document be built a second time? If the data will change, if a second audience will need it in another format, or if someone will ask “where did this number come from?”, the plain-text workflow pays for itself quickly. If none of these is likely, use whatever is fastest.

text:
Summary
Reports drift because their outputs are edited by hand. Quarto removes the copies: quarto render executes a .qmd source’s code, converts the result with Pandoc and, for PDF, typesets it with Typst, the same way every time. Add computed numbers and version control, and the Publish step is reproducible: checkable, though not automatically right. The setup pays only for documents that will be built again.
Quarto, though, renders only what it is given. In this book a coding assistant writes those sources, and its output varies from run to run and can be confidently wrong. How do you ask such a program for work, and how do you check what comes back before anything is published? Chapter 2 answers.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Assistant
text:
2.1 Model plus harness
Simon Willison, a developer, has asked most major new models the same question since 2024: “Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle”. Four Claude models, each at three effort levels, answered it with 12 drawings, and every one is recognisably a pelican on a bicycle. The dearest cost 13.09 cents, about 93 times as much as the cheapest that was good enough, at 0.14 cents (Figure 2.2).
Choosing between those drawings is the first of many judgements this chapter teaches. A coding assistant is a program that writes and edits files and runs commands at your request: you write the Prompt, it does the typing, and you Check whether the result is right. It can produce in a minute what would take an hour by hand, and it can produce plausible, confident, wrong work just as quickly. How do you get the first kind of work without being fooled by the second?
A coding assistant is two programs working together (Figure 2.1).
The model is a large language model, such as Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s GPT or Google’s Gemini. It runs on the vendor’s servers. It reads text and writes text, and it can reply with a structured request to use a tool: “read this file”, “run this command”.
The harness is the program on your computer that surrounds the model. Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are harnesses. The harness gives the model its tools (reading and writing files, running commands, searching), carries out the model’s tool requests, asks you before it does anything consequential, and sends the results back to the model. That loop repeats until the model replies with an answer instead of another request.
A short way to remember the split: the model decides, the harness does, you direct and check. It has a practical consequence. Many harnesses can run several models, so the same harness behaves differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently inside a different harness. When an assistant disappoints you, the cause can be either half, and the fix is different: a stronger model for reasoning that falls short, better rules or permissions for a harness that does the wrong thing.

Other assistants exist; this book does not test them, so it does not list them. Every prompt in the book is written to work in any of the three. A vendor’s own pairing of harness and model is the easiest to set up, but it is not automatically the best fit for a task: the assistant and the model are separate choices.

2.2.1 Pick a model by task, not by rank
Each vendor offers a family of models, from small and cheap to large and capable. They are not simply better and worse versions of one thing. Larger, more recent models usually follow longer instructions, plan multi-step work and recover from their own errors better. Small models are faster and cheaper, and often good enough for short, well-specified edits such as fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Joining two datasets or debugging a failed render rewards the stronger model.
The prompts in this book are short and specific, so a mid-sized model at a moderate effort setting (how long the model reasons before answering) is enough: Claude’s Sonnet on medium effort, or Haiku for small edits, or OpenAI’s Sol on low. For unfamiliar, hard work, the vendors’ own advice starts higher: Anthropic suggests starting with Opus 5.5 for most workloads, and OpenAI with GPT-6 Astra for complex reasoning and coding. Start small, and move up only when a task keeps failing.

Read the grid in two directions. Down the rows, the model grows and the price per token rises, so costs climb from fractions of a cent to more than ten cents. Across the columns, effort rises: the model reasons longer and writes more, so the cost usually rises while the picture gains details rather than becoming correct. Haiku on low effort has the weakest frame; from medium effort up, the frames are sound, which is consistent with, though no proof of, the book’s advice of medium effort.
Keep the evidence in proportion. It is one run per cell of one small, self-contained task, not a benchmark: run it again and you get different birds, and Fable on medium effort even cost less than Fable on low. More effort is not always better, either: at their maximum effort, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 each spent 128,000 tokens reasoning, the models’ output limit, and returned no drawing (Simon Willison’s transcripts, checked 2026-11-12). A drawing says little about a long job that joins datasets and recovers from errors, which is where stronger models earn their price. Whether a 93-fold difference in price is worth paying depends entirely on the task.

text:
2.3 What a conversation costs
Models are paid for by the token, a fragment of text of a few characters. Three things raise the cost of a session:

A bigger model costs more per token.
A higher effort setting makes the model write more reasoning tokens per reply.
A longer conversation costs more with every turn, because the model keeps no memory between requests: the harness sends the whole conversation again each time. Prompt caching makes the repeated part cheaper, not free, and caches expire.

The habits that follow are simple: a mid-sized model at moderate effort, one task per conversation, and a fresh conversation as soon as a task is done. Three commands, typed at the assistant’s prompt rather than in the shell, cover them:



Table 2.2: Three commands that control cost and context (Claude Code commands reference and Codex CLI reference, checked 2026-11-12). Type / alone to list your assistant’s commands.











Command
Claude Code
Codex
Use it when




/model
switches the model; arrows adjust the effort level where the model supports it
chooses the model and reasoning effort
a prompt keeps failing (go up) or the work is routine (go down)


/clear
starts a new conversation with empty context; the old one can be resumed
clears the terminal and starts a fresh chat
a task is finished and an unrelated one starts


/exit
exits; /quit is the same
exits; /quit is the same
you are done, or need to move to another folder






/clear matters for quality as well as cost. Old instructions and files read earlier keep steering the model while they remain in the conversation; a fresh conversation drops them. Nothing on disk changes, and the project’s rules file is read again.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. One task is finished and an unrelated one starts. Which command first?
/clear. The new task needs none of the old conversation, and carrying it along costs tokens on every turn and can mislead the model.

section: 2.4 The root folder is the assistant’s world
text:
2.4 The root folder is the assistant’s world
An assistant treats the folder you start it in as its root: it reads and edits files there and in the folders below, and runs commands from there. The first time you start one in a new folder, it asks whether you trust it. Claude Code’s prompt, captured on 2026-11-07, warns that “Claude Code’ll be able to read, edit, and execute files here”; Codex asks the same question in a folder that is a Git repository, and says it can read, edit and run files “subject to your permission settings”.
That question deserves a real answer. Trust only a folder you created for the work. Never start an assistant in your home folder, in Documents, or anywhere that holds other people’s projects, private documents or keys (such as ~/.ssh). Project instructions in a trusted folder are read and followed too, which is another reason to trust only your own folders.
Starting in a small project folder has three practical benefits. Paths in prompts stay short (data/attractions.csv), the project’s rules file is found, and a mistake stays inside one folder that you can restore. It is not a guaranteed boundary, though: a command can still name a path outside the folder, so read each command before you approve it.






WarningCommon pitfall



Two assistants writing the same files, or rendering in one folder at once, will collide; Section 6.2 shows the safe split. To work on another project, leave with /exit, change folder, and start the assistant again there.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Assistant
text:
2.5 Rules that persist: AGENTS.md
Everything you tell an assistant in conversation is forgotten when the conversation ends. Rules that must hold in every session go in a file: AGENTS.md, a plain Markdown file at the top of the project folder that the assistant reads at the start of each session. A good one has three parts:

Scope: what the project is, and what it is not.
Rules: what must always hold (“every number comes from a cited file in data/”).
Commands: how to build and check the project.

All three assistants in this book read it (checked 2026-10-30). Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work. Antigravity reads AGENTS.md or GEMINI.md in the project’s folders. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md in the working folder or above it, from version 2.1.277; a CLAUDE.md containing the line @AGENTS.md imports it, so one file can serve all three (Claude Code memory documentation, checked 2026-11-12). The repository behind this book works exactly that way: its CLAUDE.md imports its AGENTS.md.






WarningCommon pitfall



AGENTS.md is context, not enforcement. The assistant reads the rules and usually follows them, but it can still slip. Write rules that are concrete enough to check (“call ALVA counts ‘ALVA member attractions’”), and check them.


Part II writes the London guide’s rules in Chapter 4, and Part III writes the water analysis’s in Chapter 8.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Assistant
text:
2.6 How to ask for work
A prompt is the request you type into the assistant. Four habits make prompts reliable:
Be specific. Name the files, the columns, the chart type and the output. “Make a chart” invites guessing; “add a horizontal bar chart of visits_2025 by attraction from data/attractions.csv” does not.
One step at a time. One task per prompt keeps each change small enough to review, and tells you which step broke when one does.
Ask it to run and check. End with a check the assistant can perform: “render it and tell me which file it wrote”, “check that the PDF is one page”. An assistant that verifies its own work catches many of its own mistakes.
Check what changed. You are responsible for the result. Read the changed files (most assistants can show you a diff, the lines added and removed) before moving on.
The prompts in this book were designed with AI assistance and refined to reduce errors, but they are not magic, and assistants vary. When a prompt mentions something you do not understand (a YAML key, a Markdown construct, a Python call), ask before you paste:



Ask your coding assistant

Explain what a Markdown table is and when to use it. Then name the official docs page where I can verify your answer.


Asking for the documentation page matters: it turns the answer into something you can check.

2.6.1 A web chat can draft your prompt
If you know what you want but not how to ask for it, a free web chat (Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini in the browser) can turn a rough idea into a prompt. Describe the goal in plain words, name your tools, and ask for a prompt of one to four lines, with one task, concrete file names and a check (Figure 2.3). The chat cannot see your files, so it guesses; the assistant can see them, so it checks. Read the drafted prompt before you paste it, and fix any file name that does not match your folder.






Figure 2.3: A web chat drafts a prompt, you read it, and the coding assistant runs it. An illustration drawn for the workshop, not a recording: real replies vary.









WarningCommon pitfall



Paste only what you would be happy to publish. Web chats and assistants send your text to the vendor: no passwords, keys, unpublished data or personal information.

Together the boxes are one turn of the loop in the book’s title. Ask your coding assistant is the Prompt. Expect it to run and You do are where you Check, recognising each command before you approve it and opening the result yourself. The render is the Publish. Each exercise closes the loop with You’re done when: the check, stated so that you can see whether it passed.
The prompts are examples, not transcripts. Assistants vary from version to version and run to run, so the files they write will differ in detail from the ones shown. What should not vary is the result you check. Figure 2.4 shows what a session looks like.

section: 2.8 Using AI in research: say it, own it
text:
2.8 Using AI in research: say it, own it
If your work is research, using an assistant raises obligations beyond getting the code right. Journals and funders differ in detail, so read your venue’s own policy, but the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), whose recommendations many journals follow, states a common core (checked 2026-11-12):

An AI tool is never an author. Chatbots and other AI-assisted tools “should not be listed as authors because they cannot be responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of the work”.
You are responsible for what it produced. Humans are responsible for any submitted material that used AI-assisted technologies, and should review and edit AI output, which “can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased”. That includes references: AI-generated material is not an acceptable primary source.
Disclose the use. Authors describe their use of AI-assisted technologies at submission, in the cover letter and in the appropriate section of the work.

Two further rules follow from ordinary research ethics rather than from any one policy. Keep unpublished manuscripts, participant data and other confidential material out of public AI tools. And never let a tool generate or alter primary data or images: presenting generated data as observed is fabrication.
A useful disclosure names the tool and version, the tasks it performed and the checks you made. The statement for this book, on its copyright page, is written that way. Where it goes depends on the use: code and analysis belong in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce them, which in a Quarto project means the code itself and the project’s AGENTS.md.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. Which needs a statement: fixing a typo, or computing a table?
Computing a table is analysis: describe it in the Methods, in enough detail to reproduce. Venues differ on whether language editing needs a statement; ICMJE’s recommendations make no exception for it, so when in doubt, disclose.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Assistant
text:
Summary
A coding assistant is a model that decides and a harness that acts, with you directing and checking in between. Choose the model by the task: as the pelicans showed, a cheaper model at medium effort is often enough for a small, well-specified step. Cost grows with model size, effort and conversation length, so keep one task per conversation. Start the assistant only in a folder you created for the work, and put durable rules in AGENTS.md, remembering that rules are context, not enforcement. Good prompts are specific, single-step and end in a check, and every change they cause is yours to review. In research, the assistant is never an author, and its use is disclosed.
All of this assumes a computer on which an assistant, Quarto and Python are installed and working together. Is yours? Chapter 3 gets it there in six checked steps.

text:
3.1 Before you start
This chapter ends with a number: 42, printed in a web page and a PDF that your own computer built. Getting it there proves that the assistant, Python, Quarto and Typst work together. That is all Parts II and III need, because everything in them happens on your machine: the assistant writes files in your folders, Quarto renders them there, and you open the results in your own browser and word processor. It takes six steps, and each ends with a check you can see, so you always know whether a step worked before you move on.
Do the setup somewhere calm, with a good connection, and allow about an hour. Mac and Linux readers can follow this chapter straight through. Windows readers first install Ubuntu, a version of Linux, inside Windows with WSL; Appendix A walks through that one step at a time, and from then on they follow this chapter inside Ubuntu.
A stable, fast connection. Almost every step downloads something: on Windows the Ubuntu image (several hundred megabytes), then Quarto, uv and Python packages, the assistant itself and the example projects with their data. The assistant also sends every request to its model over the internet, so a weak connection shows up as long pauses, timeouts and half-finished installs, which are easy to mistake for your own errors. Use a wired connection or strong Wi-Fi, avoid VPNs where you can, and expect company networks with a proxy to block some downloads.
Two accounts. A free GitHub account, used to publish in Parts II and III, and an account with access to one coding assistant. Claude Code needs a Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise or Console account; Codex a ChatGPT sign-in or an API key; Antigravity a Google account (checked 2026-11-03). Sign-up and email verification can take hours, so do them first.
A plan for when a step fails. Errors during setup are normal: each step depends on your system, your network and that week’s versions, so an error does not mean you have failed. It tells you what to fix. Look first in Appendix D, whose Setup table lists failures seen in practice, with tested fixes. If yours is not there, use a route that does not depend on the assistant, because installs can fail before it is working, and sometimes the assistant is what fails: a web chat in your browser (Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini each have a free plan, checked 2026-11-12). Copy the command you ran and the whole error message, paste both with a sentence saying your system (“Mac”, or “Windows with Ubuntu on WSL”) and which step you are on, and try one suggested fix at a time. Read each suggested command before you run it, and never paste passwords, keys or private data. If two suggestions fail, ask a person: your group’s help channel, or a colleague.

3.2 Step 1: Get the computer ready
The later steps assume two small programs: git, for version control, and curl, for downloading. Open a terminal (on a Mac: Command-Space, type Terminal, Enter; on Ubuntu: Ctrl+Alt+T) and run the line for your system.
On a Mac, install Apple’s Command Line Tools, which include git:
xcode-select --install
A dialog asks to install them: click Install and wait. Doing this deliberately now matters, because otherwise the dialog appears the first time anything uses git, which would be in the middle of Step 4 while the assistant is waiting. “Already installed” is fine.
On Ubuntu or Debian (including Ubuntu on Windows):
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git
sudo runs a command as the administrator and asks for your Linux password, which stays invisible as you type. On other Linux distributions, install curl and git with your usual package manager. On Windows, follow Appendix A first: it ends with this same command, run inside Ubuntu.






ImportantTry it



Run git --version in the terminal.

You're done when it prints a version number. On Windows, you are in Ubuntu and wsl -l -v, run in PowerShell, shows Ubuntu with VERSION 2.

text:
3.3 Step 2: Move around the terminal
The rest of the book happens in a terminal, a window where you type commands instead of clicking. When it is ready for a command it shows a prompt, a line ending in $ (or % on a Mac), which tells you who and where you are:
ana@laptop:~/demo$
ana is the user, laptop the computer, and ~/demo the current folder: ~ is your home folder, so this is a folder called demo inside it. Eight commands are enough to move around:



Table 3.2: Moving around the terminal.









Command
Does




pwd
prints the folder you are in (print working directory)


date
prints the date and time


ls
lists what is in this folder


mkdir name
makes a folder


cd name
goes into a folder


cd ..
goes up one folder


cd ~
goes straight home, from anywhere


rmdir name
removes an empty folder (it refuses if anything is inside)






Figure 3.1 runs them in order. Type them yourself rather than pasting: the hands remember.






Figure 3.1: Moving around the terminal: each command, and what the terminal answers. A real recording, made with a demo account whose home folder is /tmp/home/ana; yours is /home/<you> on Linux and Windows, or /Users/<you> on a Mac.



Two keys save most typing mistakes: Tab completes a file or folder name, and the up arrow brings back the previous command. Later chapters use one compound command often:
mkdir -p london-guide && cd london-guide
-p makes mkdir quietly accept a folder that already exists, and && means “and then, if that worked”. Appendix B has more keys and habits.






ImportantTry it



From your home folder, type the commands in Table 3.2 in the order shown in Figure 3.1.

You're done when rmdir raised no error, and the prompt shows ~.




3.3.1 Two places to type
Once an assistant is running, there are two places to type, and mixing them up costs beginners more time than anything else.
ana@laptop:~/setup$ pwd                  <- the terminal: commands
❯ Which tools are missing?                <- the assistant: requests in plain language
The assistant takes over the terminal tab it runs in: what you type there goes to the assistant, not to the shell, until you leave with /exit. Commands in this book’s You do boxes, such as quarto preview, go in the terminal; prompts in Ask your coding assistant boxes go to the assistant. When the assistant is busy and you need the terminal, open a second tab (Ctrl+Shift+T on Ubuntu, Command-T on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+D in Windows Terminal).
Typing in the wrong place is usually harmless: a prompt typed at $ gives command not found, and a command typed into the assistant is read as a request. Look at the line you are on and try again.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. The assistant is running and the book says to type gh auth login. Where do you type it?
In a second terminal tab: gh auth login is an interactive sign-in that needs you, and the assistant is using the first tab. Leaving the assistant with /exit also works, but ends the conversation.

3.4 Step 3: Install a coding assistant
Pick one assistant and run its installer, the vendor’s own documented command (checked 2026-10-30):
# Claude Code

# Codex
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh
# Antigravity
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash

Then open a new terminal tab. A terminal learns where programs are when it starts, so it cannot find one installed a moment ago, which is the usual cause of command not found straight after an install. On a Mac, Claude Code’s installer prints a line to add to your settings under “Setup notes”: paste it, then open the new tab.

mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup

Sign in. Choose the option for your account: the first for a subscription, the second for an Anthropic Console account billed by API use. The assistant opens your browser; where there is none, as in WSL, it prints a link to copy into your browser, and then a code to paste back into the terminal.

 your team). If not, take a moment to review what's in this folder first.

3.5 Step 4: Let the assistant install the tools
The remaining tools are Quarto itself, uv (which manages Python for each project), Git and the GitHub command-line tool gh. Each has its own official install method for each system, which is exactly the kind of detail an assistant handles well. Start it again in the setup folder:



You do

mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup && claude



Ask your coding assistant

Check which of `git`, `curl`, `uv`, `quarto` (1.10 or newer) and the GitHub CLI `gh` are missing on this computer. Install only those, using each tool's official method for my system. Never run `sudo`, or an installer that asks for a password, yourself: print each such command alone in a code block, using full paths, then wait until I say done. Then print every version.



Expect it to run

installs uv with its official installer · Quarto from its release page (or Homebrew on a Mac) · gh from GitHub’s own package source · prints versions


The prompt is written around one limitation: an assistant cannot type your password. So it asks the assistant to hand back any command that needs one, with full paths, because the second tab you paste it into starts in your home folder. Paste the command there, type your password when sudo asks (it stays invisible), and then type done in the assistant’s tab. On a Mac, the password is your login password.






NoteWhy this works



Quarto has no Ubuntu package in the standard repositories, and Ubuntu’s own gh package is discouraged by GitHub, so a generic apt install would get one tool wrong and the other missing. The prompt’s “each tool’s official method” sends the assistant to the right source for each (Quarto’s download page and GitHub’s install instructions for Linux, checked 2026-10-30).








ImportantTry it



Paste the prompt, approve the commands you have read, and run any sudo command it hands you in a second tab.

You're done when it prints a version for all five tools. Then type /exit: uv and Quarto are only found by a terminal started after they were installed.

3.6 Step 5: Run the setup check
Open a new tab and start the assistant again, so that it sees the newly installed tools:



You do

cd ~/setup && claude



Ask your coding assistant

Print the versions of `quarto` (1.10 or newer), `uv`, `gh` and this assistant, and run `quarto check` (no Jupyter or LaTeX yet is fine: count it as OK). If `git config --global user.name` or `user.email` is unset, ask me for my name and my GitHub email, then set them. Clone https://github.com/project-delphi/quarto-workshop.git to `~/quarto-workshop` (if it exists, `git pull` only when its working tree is clean) and list its `checkpoints/`. Run `gh auth status`. Run every check even if one fails, then report each as OK or not.


Three parts of this check deserve a word.
quarto check reports Quarto’s own components, including Pandoc and Typst. Its Python and Jupyter lines may say they are missing, and that is fine: each project in this book gets its own Python environment from uv, so there is nothing to install for Python now. No LaTeX is needed either, because PDFs are made with the Typst engine bundled in Quarto.
A fresh Git has no identity, and git commit refuses to run without one. The prompt makes the assistant ask you for your name and email, so you type your own; check that what it set is yours, not a placeholder.
The clone brings the workshop repository to ~/quarto-workshop. It holds the finished examples, the water dataset and the checkpoints: snapshots of each project at the end of each hands-on block, which you will use to catch up if you fall behind.



You do

if gh is not “Logged in”: in a second tab, gh auth login → GitHub.com → HTTPS → Yes → log in with a web browser; copy the one-time code to github.com/login/device; then ask the assistant to check gh again

Run the setup check.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
3.7 Step 6: The test run
The setup check proves the tools are installed. The test run proves they work together: the assistant can write a file and run commands you approve, uv can build a project environment, Quarto can run Python through it, and Typst can write a PDF.



You do

mkdir -p ~/quarto-test && cd ~/quarto-test
claude



Ask your coding assistant

Run `uv init --bare` and `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml`. Create hello.qmd (html and typst formats): a Python cell computing `6 * 7` and an inline-code sentence showing it. Render it with `uv run quarto render hello.qmd`; check hello.html and hello.pdf both say 42.



Expect it to run

uv init --bare · uv add … · writes hello.qmd · uv run quarto render hello.qmd → hello.html, hello.pdf



You do

/exit, then open the folder: open . (Mac), xdg-open . (Linux) or explorer.exe . (WSL), and open both files


The test run uses things the next chapters explain, YAML settings, a code cell and inline code, on purpose: it is a black-box check that the tools work together, not a lesson. If you are curious, hello.qmd is the file shown in Section 1.2.

Every render prints a line such as [IPKernelApp] WARNING | Kernel is running over TCP without encryption. London’s tourism office has one set of facts and many readers. Visitors want a web page they can open on a phone. text:
4.4 Rules for the guide
Section 2.5 introduced AGENTS.md, the file of rules an assistant reads at the start of every session. The guide needs one now, before any data or photos arrive, because every later prompt relies on it:



Ask your coding assistant

Create AGENTS.md for this project. Scope: a London visitor guide for the tourism office, written once and reused for every audience. Rules: every number comes from a cited file in data/, photos are openly licensed, credited and show no people, never invent facts, keep data/ and images/ unchanged, and call ALVA counts "ALVA member attractions". Show me the file.



Expect it to run

writes AGENTS.md: a scope and a list of rules



You do

approve · read it: does it say what you meant?


Each rule is there for a reason the project will meet. Every number comes from a cited file: the guide quotes visitor counts, and an assistant asked for a number it does not have may produce a plausible one; a rule that every figure is computed from a file with a source removes that temptation, and gives you something to check. Openly licensed photos with no people: a published guide needs images it may reuse, and pictures of identifiable people raise consent questions it does not need. Keep data/ and images/ unchanged: the inputs are evidence, and edits belong in the analysis, not in the evidence. “ALVA member attractions”: the counts come from the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions, which lists only its members, so “London’s most visited attractions” would overclaim.
The finished project’s version reads, in part:
## Rules

- Every number comes from a cited file in `data/`: each row carries `source`, `url` and
  `retrieved`. Never estimate or invent a figure or a fact.
- ALVA counts only its member sites: write "ALVA member attractions".
- Photos are openly licensed, credited from `images/ATTRIBUTION.md`, and show no people.
- Keep `data/` and `images/` unchanged.
Read what the assistant wrote and edit it yourself if the wording is off. It is your project’s contract with the assistant, and the rules work best when they are concrete enough to check.

section: 4.9 An environment for the code to come
text:
4.9 An environment for the code to come
The next chapter runs Python, and code never runs in a vacuum. It runs on an operating system (macOS, Windows, Linux) and a processor (Intel and AMD x86_64, or Apple and other ARM arm64), in some version of its language, with packages at particular versions. Many scientific Python packages contain compiled C, C++ or Fortran, built separately for each system and processor, and Python’s packaging encodes both in each package file’s platform tag, such as macosx_11_0_arm64 (Python Packaging Authority, checked 2026-10-31).
Getting all of that to agree used to be a lesson of its own: install conda or a system Python, sometimes a compiler, fix the PATH, register a Jupyter kernel, then debug it on every laptop. uv now does it in one step, for one project at a time. It fetches the Python version a project needs, and its lockfile, uv.lock, “captures the packages that would be installed across all possible Python markers such as operating system, architecture, and Python version” (uv documentation, checked 2026-10-31), so one file reproduces the same environment on every Mac, Windows and Linux machine. Other languages pair a project file with a lockfile in the same way: R’s renv.lock, JavaScript’s package-lock.json, Rust’s Cargo.lock.



Ask your coding assistant

Give this folder its own Python environment with `uv`: run `uv init --bare`, then `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml pandas matplotlib plotly`. From now on run `quarto` and `python` through `uv run`, and add that rule to AGENTS.md. Show me the Python line of `uv run quarto check jupyter`.



Expect it to run

writes pyproject.toml (the packages), uv.lock (their exact versions) and .venv/ (the installed environment) · adds a rule to AGENTS.md








Figure 4.4: Giving the guide its own environment: uv init --bare, uv add with the guide’s packages, and Quarto finding the project’s own Python. A real recording with a demo account; the 40-second first render of the engine check is cut.



The four packages ipykernel, nbclient, nbformat and pyyaml are what Quarto needs to run Python cells; pandas, matplotlib and plotly are what the guide’s code will use. The larger jupyter package, with its notebook applications, is not needed. Measured in a dry run on 2026-10-30, on one fast connection, a cold install of Part III’s larger package set took 8 seconds with uv and 31 seconds with pip plus jupyter. That compares the old route with the new one, not the two installers like for like, since the pip run also installed jupyter.






NoteWhy this works



Why uv run in front of every command? Quarto refuses to run Python next to a .venv folder that is not activated (“There is an unactivated Python environment in .venv”). uv run activates the project’s environment for that one command, and first brings .venv up to date with uv.lock. So a copied project, or a checkpoint, rebuilds its own environment on its first uv run, and the rule in AGENTS.md keeps the assistant using it after a restart.








ImportantTry it



Run the environment prompt. Keep the preview running: london.md needs no Python yet.

You're done when uv run quarto check jupyter reports the Python in this folder’s .venv.

title: 5  Documents That Compute
text:
5.1 Settings at the top: the title block
In 2024, by ALVA’s count, the most visited of the guide’s five sights was the British Museum, with 6,479,952 visits; in 2025, the Natural History Museum, with 7,116,929. A guide that said, in typed words, that the British Museum is the most visited of the five went on saying it after ALVA published its 2025 table, in every copy, until someone noticed.
This chapter makes the guide compute instead. Code reads the data at every render, so a new table corrects every sentence, the chart drawn from it, and the Word and PDF versions at once, without a single number copied by hand. That is the workflow’s central promise, and the rest of the book builds on it.
Front matter is a block of settings between two lines of three dashes at the very top of a file. It is written in YAML, a format for settings in which indentation is meaning: nested settings are indented by two spaces, and a wrong indent changes what a setting belongs to. A .qmd file is Markdown plus front matter plus code; the extension tells Quarto to look for both.

5.2 Numbers the guide computes



Ask your coding assistant

In london.qmd, add a Python cell that reads data/attractions.csv and finds the most visited attraction and total visits_2025, plus a sentence showing both with inline code. The preview re-renders it: check london.html.


The assistant writes a code cell, a code fence whose language is in braces, and a sentence that uses its results:
```{python}
import pandas as pd
attractions = pd.read_csv("data/attractions.csv")
top = attractions.loc[attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
top_name = top["attraction"]
top_visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"
total_visits = f"{attractions['visits_2025'].sum():,}"
```

Most visited in 2025: the `{python} top_name`, with `{python} top_visits` visits.
London's ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew `{python} total_visits` visits.
When the document renders, the cell runs and its variables are kept; each `{python} name` is inline code, replaced by the value of name. Rendered in this book from the same data file, the sentence reads:

Most visited in 2025: the Natural History Museum (South Kensington), with 7,116,929 visits. London’s ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew 39,692,434 visits.

Quarto 1.4 introduced this inline syntax, one for every engine, Python included; R users already wrote inline code with knitr’s `r x`, a syntax Quarto still supports (Quarto 1.4 release notes, checked 2026-11-12).






TipIn practice



Pause and think. If attractions.csv changes, which numbers in the sentence update?
All three: the top attraction’s name, its visits and the total, because each is computed from the file. They update at the next render, not when the file is saved. Anything typed by hand does not update at all.


The figures come from ALVA’s table of visits made in 2025 to its member attractions, retrieved on 2026-10-30. Only ALVA’s members are counted, which is why the sentence says “ALVA member attractions”: the project’s rules made the assistant write it that way.

1

A label starting fig- numbers the figure and lets the text refer to it as @fig-top10, which renders as “Figure 1” with a link.

2

3

The caption, shown under the figure.

4

The alt text, read aloud by screen readers.


Figure 5.1 is that chart, drawn by this book from the same file. Notice that its caption and alt text describe different things: the caption says what the chart is, the alt text says what it shows.








Figure 5.1: Visits in 2025 to London’s ten most visited ALVA member attractions.





Matplotlib draws a static image, so the same figure travels to every format: web page, Word, PDF, slides. Interactive charts, such as Plotly’s, are JavaScript that runs in a browser, so they belong in web pages and dashboards (Chapter 6) and not in a PDF.

Ask your coding assistant

The front matter’s format becomes a list:
format:
  html:
1    format-links:
      - docx
2      - {format: typst, text: PDF}
  docx: default
3  typst: default

1

format-links adds a download link to the web page for each other format listed.

2

An entry can be a format name, or an object with the format and the link’s text.

3

typst makes the PDF with the Typst engine inside Quarto; no LaTeX is involved.


One quarto render now writes three files. Each format runs the code cells again, so the inline numbers and the figure appear in every file without anything being copied. To render only one format, add --to docx (or --to typst).






NoteWhy this works

Re-running is the price of each format getting output made for it. For a slow analysis, the cure is to compute once in a script and have every format read the results, which is exactly how Part III is built (Section 8.6).

text:
5.6 What a render does, and why two renders collide
Figure 1.1 in Section 1.2 showed the three steps of a render. With code in the document, the first step is worth looking at more closely, because it explains the commonest failure of this chapter.
To run the cells, Quarto writes the document out as a temporary Jupyter notebook, named after the file (london.quarto_ipynb), starts a Python kernel (a running Python process) from the project’s environment, sends it each cell in order, and collects the results. Two consequences follow. The cells share one Python session, top to bottom, so a later cell can use a variable from an earlier one, and the order of cells matters. And two renders of the same file at the same moment write the same temporary files, which is why a render started while a preview is re-rendering fails with readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'.
Every render runs every cell again. That is deliberate in this book’s projects: they set freeze: false, so outputs always match the data. It also means a slow cell slows every render; Chapter 14 returns to the trade-off and to freeze: auto, which caches results and needs a rule for when to throw them away.
Each render also prints the harmless IPKernelApp warning described in Section 3.7.






ImportantTry it



Stop the preview, then add the formats with the prompt in Section 5.4 (and, if you like, the optional three).

You're done when london.docx and london.pdf show the computed sentence and the chart (and, with the optional formats, so do the slides, the PowerPoint deck and the e-book).

6.1 Content once, format per audience
Correct one fact, then count the documents that repeat it. Written by hand, a dashboard, a partner brief and a printed flyer each hold their own copy of the same facts, and every copy has to be found and fixed. The one that is missed is the one that disagrees in public.
This chapter writes all three in one step: a dashboard for managers, a Word brief and its covering email for partners, and a flyer for walk-ins. The dashboard and the brief read the same data file, so a corrected count reaches both; the flyer copies its facts from data/sights.csv, a choice Section 7.5 returns to. None of the three needs another to exist, which makes them the first job in this book worth splitting across several assistants at once, and the first chance to ask when that is worth what it costs.
Each audience gets the format that suits it, and each format is a setting:
A dashboard is a page of charts and key numbers arranged in a grid. In a .qmd file with format: dashboard, a level-1 heading starts a page, a level-2 heading starts a row, and each cell’s output becomes a card in that row (Quarto dashboards documentation, checked 2026-10-31). The guide’s dashboard has two pages:
It also needs a second data file. data/visits.csv holds the yearly visits to the five sights from 2015 to 2025, from ALVA’s annual tables. Two notes travel with it, from the data’s README. The years 2020 and 2021 are pandemic years, not comparable with the others. And from 2024 the Natural History Museum’s count includes its reopened gardens, so for that museum 2024 and 2025 are not like-for-like with earlier years. data/churches.csv lists the ten cathedrals and churches on Visit London’s own list, an editorial choice with no visitor numbers.
A Word brief turns Markdown headings into Word’s heading styles, so the partner’s copy has a navigable outline and working links. Its covering email is not rendered at all: it is a plain Markdown file whose message sits in a text block, to be copied into an email client, with the brief attached. The email deliberately quotes no visitor numbers. The numbers stay in the brief, where they are computed and cited, as the project’s rules require.
A flyer is a one-page Typst PDF on A5 paper. papersize accepts any of Typst’s paper names (a5, a4, us-letter and so on), and margin sets the margins (Quarto’s Typst documentation, checked 2026-10-30).

6.2 Sub-agents: one lead, many hands
The three outputs are independent: none needs another to exist. That makes them a candidate for sub-agents, separate assistant sessions that your assistant starts for one task each (Figure 6.3). Each sub-agent has its own context, does its task and reports back; your assistant, the lead, waits for all of them and then checks the results.






Figure 6.3: One lead, three sub-agents. Each writes only its own files and renders nothing; the lead renders the files one at a time.



The gain is time: three independent tasks take about as long as the slowest of them. The cost is tokens, because each sub-agent does its own reading, reasoning and tool calls. The three assistants differ in how they offer it (all checked 2026-10-31). Claude Code starts sub-agents in parallel when a prompt asks for them. Codex enables sub-agents by default and starts them when asked, and its documentation warns both that parallel edits “can create conflicts” and that sub-agent runs use more tokens. Antigravity’s command-line agent can delegate to parallel sub-agents, but its documentation does not say a prompt can require it, so it may do the tasks itself.
Two rules make parallel work safe, and the prompt below states both. Each sub-agent writes only its own files and renders nothing, so no two of them touch the same file. The lead renders the files one at a time, because two Quarto renders, or two environment updates by uv run, in the same folder can collide. Sub-agents read AGENTS.md too, so the project’s rules still apply to their work.






TipIn practice



Use sub-agents when tasks are independent, substantial and write different files. Do not use them for tasks where one needs another’s result, for several edits to the same file, or for small tasks where the overhead of starting and briefing a sub-agent outweighs the work. A prompt that might run without sub-agents should say what to do then: the prompt below ends its first sentence with “none? do the items in turn”.

title: 7  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
7.1 Git: every change, safely
The guide is finished, and nobody but you can see it: every output sits in a folder on your computer. This chapter puts it on the web, where anyone can open it on a phone, with Git to keep every version of the source and GitHub Pages to serve the result. Then it asks the question the whole workflow is built to answer: if one input changes, which outputs change with it, and how do you know? That question comes with no prompt. It tests whether you can predict what a rebuild will do, and then check.
Chapter 1 likened Git to Word’s Track Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history. In practice that means two things. You see exactly what changed, line by line, and someone else can approve it before it counts. And every earlier version of the whole project is kept, with a note saying why it changed, so any of them can be restored or compared.
The vocabulary is short (Figure 7.1; Pro Git and GitHub’s documentation, checked 2026-10-31). A repository is a project folder with its history; each saved version is a commit, a snapshot of every tracked file with its message.
A branch is a movable label on a line of commits, so work can go on there while the main line, main, keeps working. To push is to copy commits to the shared repository on GitHub. A pull request proposes merging a branch and shows the difference, or diff, line by line; a review comments on it, approves it or asks for changes; merging adds its commits to main.
Working alone, as in this book, you commit straight to main and push; in a team, every change goes round the loop. Either way the assistant runs the Git commands and you approve them. Ask it to “commit with a message that says why”, and read its diffs before you approve: a diff is the clearest check you have of what the assistant actually did.

7.2 Where a site lives
A rendered Quarto website is static: a folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and documents, with no program running on a server. Any web server can serve it, so publishing means copying that folder to a host. GitHub Pages is the host this book uses, because the repository is already on GitHub and quarto publish gh-pages is built in (Figure 7.2).






Figure 7.2: Publishing to GitHub Pages. The source goes to the main branch with Git; quarto publish gh-pages renders the site on your computer and pushes only the rendered HTML to a separate branch, which GitHub serves.



There are two ways to get a site onto a host. Either you render on your own computer and upload the result, as quarto publish does for GitHub Pages and Netlify, or the host builds the site from your repository on every push. The second works only if the build installs Quarto, Python and every package the project needs, or if the rendered output is committed. The London repository leaves its rendered _site/ folder out, so a host that builds would produce nothing until the build is set up.

The first publish is yours, typed in the terminal. It asks one question, then renders the site, creates the gh-pages branch, pushes the rendered site and opens it. text:
7.5 Change one input, explain the rebuild
Chapter 1 began with a correction (Section 1.1): ALVA revises one figure, and in a copy-and-paste workflow someone has to carry it by hand into every file that quotes it. Here is that scenario for real, in a project where no visitor count was ever copied. No prompt is supplied: write your own, or do it by hand.






ImportantTry it




Predict. Set the Tower of London’s visits_2025 in data/attractions.csv to 8000000. Which outputs will change?
Rebuild the site.
Explain which outputs changed, which did not, and why.
Undo: git restore data/attractions.csv, then rebuild, so no trial number stays in your files.

Make the edit yourself (for example nano data/attractions.csv; Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X to save and leave): the project’s rules keep the assistant out of data/, which is the point of them.

title: 7  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
Summary
Git keeps every version of the source as commits; teams move each change through branch, pull request, review and merge. A rendered site is static files that any host can serve, and quarto publish gh-pages fills GitHub Pages from your own computer, interactively the first time. A _quarto.yml with an explicit render list makes a folder a website. When an input changes, every page whose code loads it updates at the next render, in every format; copied facts do not, and neither does the live site until you publish again.
That completes one guide for many audiences. In Part III the hard part is the analysis itself: grouping Colombia’s municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context. That one analysis is then published as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all reading the results of one script, and its rebuild test changes a setting of the analysis instead of a number in a table.

title: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications
text:
Where Colombia’s tap water is tested, the countryside’s is far riskier than the towns’. In 2023, of the rural zones (a municipality’s countryside, outside its head town) with a utility-supplied water-risk score, 28% fell in the high-risk or unfit bands, against 6% of urban ones. And much rural water has no score at all: that year, 6.8 million of the 12.6 million people in rural zones lived where the open data hold none.
This part asks which kinds of municipal zone exist, judged by water safety, services and context, and how infant mortality, exam scores and school dropout differ between those kinds. You are the analyst. Your readers are officials, who need a report, and a municipal council, which needs slides, and both deserve an answer that says plainly what the data cannot show:

8  The Question, the Data and the Rules pins down what is asked, what the data mean and what the assistant may not do.
9  Look Before You Model finds where the data are empty or misleading, and meets Tunja, the municipality this part follows.
10  From Table to Features turns the table into features a clustering can use, and counts the cost.
11  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means lets an algorithm group the zone-years, and decides how many groups there are.
12  Interpreting Clusters names the kinds and compares their outcomes.
13  Correlation Is Not Causation asks whether worse water goes with more infant deaths, and why that is not a cause.
14  Publish Many turns one set of results into a report, slides, a blog post and a website.

The exercises at the end of the part test whether you can do it without the prompts.



Where we are: Part III.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.1 The question and its readers
In 2023, Colombia’s national report on drinking water scored the water of its urban areas at 5.7, in the low-risk band, and the water of its rural areas at 36.5, in the high-risk band (Table 8.1). DANE’s projections put 12.6 million people, 24% of the population, in rural zones in 2023. People drink and cook with this water, so where the risk sits, and what goes with it, is worth knowing.
The question for this part is therefore: which kinds of municipal zone exist in Colombia, judged by water safety, services and context, and how do health and education outcomes differ between them? Part II’s numbers were simple counts; these are not. Every step has a way to go wrong that a clean render will not reveal: a variable that means something narrower than its name, a gap that is not random, a comparison that looks causal and is not. This chapter deals with all three before any code is written, and ends with the rules that hold the assistant to them.
The question splits in two, and the order matters:
“Kinds” will be clusters: groups of zone-years that are similar to each other on the chosen variables, found by an algorithm called k-means (Chapter 11). Because the unit is a zone in a year, a municipality’s two zones can belong to different kinds, and a zone can move between kinds over the years.
The answer has two readers. Officials will read it as a report, in Word or as a PDF, and a municipal council will see it as a short deck of slides (Chapter 14). Both will look for where to act, and both will be tempted to read a difference between kinds as an effect of the water. So the limits are stated now, each with its reason. The water score covers only systems run by a utility (Section 8.2). Many rural zones have no score at all, so the results describe sampled systems (Section 9.2). And the comparisons describe; they cannot establish that water causes any outcome (Chapter 13).

8.2 Scoring water risk: the IRCA
Colombia scores the safety of drinking water with the IRCA, the Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano (water-quality risk index for human consumption), defined in Resolución 2115 of 2007. It runs from 0, every test passed, to 100, every test failed, and article 15 sorts the scale into five bands (Table 8.1).



Table 8.1: The IRCA risk bands (Resolución 2115 de 2007, art. 15) and where the 2023 national figures fall (MinSalud, MinVivienda, INS and Superservicios, INCA 2023, Bogotá, January 2025, Tabla 4; both checked 2026-10-30).

The national average sits in the medium band and hides the urban–rural gap, which is why this part’s data keep each municipality’s two zones apart.






NoteWhy this works



Surveillance samples of tap water are tested against health limits. Each tested characteristic carries a risk score: Escherichia coli 25, total coliforms 15, turbidity 15, free residual chlorine 15, apparent colour 6 and pH 1.5, among others. A sample’s IRCA is the score of the characteristics that fail their limit, as a percentage of the score of all those tested, and a month’s IRCA is the mean over its samples (articles 13 and 14). That is why 0 means every test passed and 100 means every test failed.








WarningCommon pitfall



The IRCA in this part’s data is not the national figure. The open table it comes from (INS, datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3) holds the utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA: samples from systems run by a water utility. A check on 2026-10-30 found that its 2023 department totals match INCA’s utility column in 30 of 30 departments and the overall figure in only 5. Self-supplied systems, which have no utility, score far worse (43.7 against 7.4 in 2023), so the data understate the risk wherever people rely on self-supply, and say nothing where no utility exists. Label the variable “utility-supplied IRCA” everywhere it appears.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.3 Two measures: IRCA and Saber 11
The outcomes the analysis compares include an education measure, Saber 11, the national exam taken by students finishing upper secondary school, set by ICFES. It has five tests: critical reading, mathematics, social studies and citizenship, natural sciences, and English. The global score is five times the weighted mean of the five test scores (each 0 to 100; English counts once, the others three times), from 0 to 500, and its mean was fixed at 250 in the first sitting in 2014, so that years can be compared (ICFES, Guía de orientación Saber 11.° 2017-1, pp. 101 and 104, checked 2026-10-30).
Both measures are averages, and an average describes only what it averaged over. IRCA is an average over the water samples taken, so a system that is never sampled has no IRCA at all. The Saber 11 mean in the data is an average over the students who sat the exam at schools in that municipality and zone, so it says nothing about students who had left school. Keep both facts in mind in every comparison that follows.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.4 Where the data come from
Most of the data are Colombian open data from five public bodies; rainfall and altitude come from two scientific datasets. All are joined on DANE’s DIVIPOLA municipality codes:

INS (Instituto Nacional de Salud): the IRCA surveillance results.
DANE (the national statistics office): the list of municipalities and their codes, population projections and municipal boundaries.
ICFES and MEN (the Ministry of Education): Saber 11 results and school dropout rates.
DNP (the National Planning Department), through its TerriData portal: water and sewer coverage, multidimensional poverty, municipal performance, transfers for water and infant mortality.
CHIRPS (the Climate Hazards Center’s rainfall data) and NASA SRTM (elevation data): rainfall, and a derived altitude for each head town.

They arrive as three files, in examples/water/data/ in the workshop repository: water_municipal.csv (the analysis table), municipios.geojson (municipal boundaries for maps) and README.md, which documents every column, source, licence and caveat (Appendix G lists them all).
One row is one municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year. The urban zone is the head town (cabecera municipal); the rural zone is the smaller settlements and the dispersed countryside. The table covers every one of DANE’s 1,122 DIVIPOLA entries, both zones and every year from 2010 to 2023: 31,416 rows and 29 columns. Of those entries, 1,103 are municipalities; the rest are the island of San Andrés and areas that are not municipalities, whose rows are mostly empty. Because every municipality has all its rows, a gap is an empty cell, never a missing row.






TipIn practice



Read data/README.md before you analyse anything, and ask the assistant to read it first too. Its caveats are the analysis’s traps, written down: the IRCA source above; department capitals that have no urban and rural split for coverage; a fiscal index whose method changes in 2020; infant mortality whose method changes in 2017; Saber 11 only in some years; pesos that are not adjusted for inflation. Each one turns up in the chapters that follow.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.5 Features and outcomes
The most important design decision in Part III is which variables define the kinds and which only describe them.
The features, which the clustering sees, are 9 variables about water, people and place, and government: the utility-supplied IRCA, piped water and sewer coverage, the 2018 census’s multidimensional poverty index, the rural share of the population, the head town’s altitude, rainfall, a municipal performance index (MDM), and transfers for water per person (SGP, on a log scale). The outcomes, which the analysis only compares, are infant mortality, the Saber 11 score and school dropout.
Never cluster on an outcome. If infant mortality helped define the kinds, the kinds would differ in infant mortality by construction, and the comparison in the second question would be circular: it would find exactly what was put in. Keeping outcomes out of the clustering is what lets the comparison say anything at all.






NoteWhy this works



The same care is why the fiscal index idf is not a feature, although it describes municipal government: its method changes in 2020 (idf to 2020, idf_new from 2020, on different scales), so it cannot form one series across the years the analysis uses. A variable that changes meaning partway through would create kinds that are artefacts of the change.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.6 Compute once, publish many
Part II computed in each page. Part III computes once (Figure 8.1). One importable script, scripts/analysis.py, does all of the computation and writes its results to outputs/; every page only reads those results and draws them. A design choice, such as how many rows to drop for missing values, is made in one place, and every output follows at the next render.






Figure 8.1: Compute once, publish many. One script turns the data into results once; every publication reads the results, and none recomputes them.



The split solves two problems from Part II. A slow computation no longer slows every page and every format, because it runs once. And no page can disagree with another, because there is only one result to disagree with. Results are saved as Parquet, which keeps column types (a code such as 05001 stays text instead of becoming the number 5001), and as CSV where people will open them.
This book follows the same rule: every number in Part III is computed when the book is built, by importing the finished project’s analysis.py and running it in memory.

section: 8.7 Setting up the project: data, rules and environment
text:
8.7 Setting up the project: data, rules and environment
The project lives beside the London one, so that the workshop repository’s checkpoints are always at ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/:
~                      your home folder
├── quarto-workshop/   the clone from Chapter 3
├── london-guide/      Part II
└── water-quality/     this part's project
Make the folder, start the assistant in it, and copy the data:



You do

cd ~ && mkdir -p water-quality && cd water-quality
claude



Ask your coding assistant

Copy ../quarto-workshop/examples/water/data into this folder as data/, then list the files in data/ with their sizes.


Then write the rules. If you have never clustered anything, the worry is fair: the assistant can write an analysis that runs, renders and is wrong. You do not guard against that by writing the code yourself. You guard against it by checking, and a check needs something to check against.



Ask your coding assistant

Read data/README.md, then create AGENTS.md for this project. Scope: describe Colombian municipal water safety and infant mortality from data/ only. Rules: keep data/ unchanged, label IRCA as utility-supplied (prestadores), never cluster on outcomes, and say comparisons are descriptive, not causal. Show me the file.



Expect it to run

reads data/README.md · writes AGENTS.md: scope, rules, the data’s caveats


The four rules are this chapter in miniature: the inputs are evidence and stay unchanged; the IRCA is labelled for what it is; outcomes describe the clusters but never define them; and comparisons between clusters do not establish causal effects of water safety. Asking the assistant to read the README first lets it add the data’s caveats to the rules itself.



Ask your coding assistant

Give this project its own Python environment with `uv`: run `uv init --bare`, then `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml pandas numpy matplotlib plotly scikit-learn pyarrow itables tabulate`. Run `quarto` and `python` through `uv run`, and add that rule to AGENTS.md. Show me the Python line of `uv run quarto check jupyter`.


The recipe is the London guide’s, with the analysis’s packages added: scikit-learn for k-means, pyarrow for Parquet, itables for the dashboard’s searchable table and tabulate for tables written as Markdown. Packages shared with Part II come from uv’s cache.
