title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
Summary
The question is which kinds of municipal zone exist in Colombia, by water safety, services and context, and how outcomes differ between them; its readers, officials and a municipal council, need the limits stated as plainly as the results. IRCA scores tap-water samples from 0 (no risk) to 100 (unfit), in five official bands; the data’s IRCA is the utility-supplied figure, which understates risk wherever people rely on self-supply; and both IRCA and Saber 11 average only over what was measured. One row is a municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year, every row exists, and gaps are empty cells. Nine features define the kinds and three outcomes only describe them, because clustering on an outcome makes the comparison circular. One script computes everything once, and the project’s rules write these decisions down for the assistant. What the rules cannot say is what the table holds: where it is empty, and where a series moves for reasons unrelated to water. That is the next chapter’s question.

9.1 What exploring is for
Before any model, look at the data. Exploring tells you what a model will and will not be able to see: which columns are sparse, which zones are never measured, and whether a series changes level for reasons that have nothing to do with the thing it measures. None of that shows up as an error. A clustering algorithm will happily group rows that have been made comparable only by filling their gaps, and a chart of a series whose method changed will draw a trend that is not there.
The water data hold two such surprises that a chart can show, and several more that show only up close, in one place. For those, this chapter meets Tunja, the municipality the rest of the part follows. Then the assistant builds the project’s first page, explore.qmd, and you check it against what you have already seen.
Four questions are worth answering before modelling any table, and this chapter asks each of them of the water data:
The answers decide what the analysis can claim. If one group is mostly missing, conclusions about it rest on the minority that was measured, and that minority may not be typical.

9.2 Rural: less data, more risk








Figure 9.1: All rows, 2010–2023, by zone: no IRCA reported (hatched) and the Resolución 2115 risk band of the rest. Utility-supplied IRCA, INS open data (datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3).





Side by side, Figure 9.1 shows all 31,416 rows. 53% of rural rows have no IRCA at all, against 14% of urban rows, because many rural systems are never sampled, or are not run by a utility and so fall outside the utility-supplied table. Among the rural rows that do have a value, 51% fall in the high or unfit bands, against 12% of urban rows.
The two facts compound, in the worst direction: the zones whose scores are worse are also the ones least often scored. The gaps are not missing at random: they depend on zone, and perhaps on the risk itself. Any analysis that drops the rows without IRCA, as Part III’s must, describes sampled rural systems only, and should say so.








Figure 9.2: Median utility-supplied IRCA by year and zone, 2010–2023, over the rows that report one.





The fourth question matters, as Figure 9.2 shows. The rural median drops sharply in 2016 and again in 2020. That could be an improvement in rural water, or a change in which systems were sampled; the data’s README warns that the 2020 drop may reflect sampling, and the open data cannot tell the two apart. An analysis that compares years should not read the drop as progress without evidence from outside the table.

Aggregates hide the details that make a variable trustworthy or not, so from here on this part follows one municipality through every step. title: 10  From Table to Features
text:
10.1 Four steps from table to features
A clustering algorithm does not read a table the way a person does. It sees numbers, measures distances between rows, and groups rows that are close. Everything about the result depends on which rows it sees, which numbers, on what scale, and what it is given where a number is missing. Preparation is the name for those decisions, and they shape the clusters as much as the algorithm does. Four of them stand between the water table and the clustering. Each has a price, counted here in rows and in guesses, before the assistant writes all four into scripts/analysis.py, the one script that every later page reads.
1. Select. Keep the years 2016 to 2023, because the municipal performance index (MDM), one of the features, starts in 2016. Keep municipalities only: San Andrés has none of DNP’s values and the non-municipalised areas are nearly empty. Keep only rows with an IRCA value, since water safety is the point of the analysis.
2. Transform. Transfers for water per person (SGP) are heavily skewed, with a few very large values, so the analysis uses their logarithm. Department capitals have no urban and rural split for coverage, so their urban rows use the municipality’s total coverage instead, and a flag column records that they did.
3. Impute, with flags. Drop rows missing more than two of the nine features. Fill the remaining gaps with the median of the same year and zone, and add a flag column, such as water_coverage_imputed, that marks every filled value.
4. Standardise within each year. Replace each feature by its z-score within its year:
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}_{\text{year}}}{s_{\text{year}}}\]
where \(\bar{x}_{\text{year}}\) and \(s_{\text{year}}\) are the feature’s mean and standard deviation over that year’s kept rows. A z-score of +1 means one standard deviation above that year’s average.

title: 10  From Table to Features
text:
NoteWhy this works



Why within each year rather than over all years? Two reasons. SGP is in nominal pesos, not adjusted for inflation, so its values drift upwards over time for reasons unrelated to any municipality. And other features shift as a whole from year to year. Standardising within each year removes both shifts, so a single clustering over all years gives labels that mean the same relative position in every year: a zone is compared with that year’s other zones, so a nationwide shift, real or an artefact of sampling, does not move it between clusters.








WarningCommon pitfall



Every fill is a guess, and an unflagged guess becomes indistinguishable from data. The flags make the guesses countable and checkable later: a cluster made mostly of imputed values would be a cluster of medians, not of places. The rule of the project, from its AGENTS.md: nothing is filled silently.

title: 10  From Table to Features
text:
10.3 Why scale?
k-means groups rows by straight-line, or Euclidean, distance: the square root of the sum of squared differences across the features. A feature’s share of the expected squared distance, between two rows picked at random, is proportional to its variance. In raw units, the features measured in thousands, such as millimetres of rain and metres of altitude, dwarf those measured from 0 to 100 (Figure 10.1).








Figure 10.1: Each feature’s share of the squared distance between rows, in raw units and after z-scores. Kept rows, 2016–2023.





Unscaled, rainfall and altitude together would make up 99.8% of the distance, so the clusters would be climate zones and the water variables would hardly count. After z-scores, every feature has variance 1 and contributes the same share, about 11%. The log of SGP matters too. In raw pesos, its variance would be about 3,100 times rainfall’s, so it would dominate even rainfall; after z-scores, the log keeps a few very large transfers from sitting far from every other row, cutting the largest z-score from 7.3 to 4.3.






TipIn practice



Equal weight is itself a choice, not a neutral default. Nine z-scored features count equally, so the three safety-and-coverage variables count for 33% of the distance and context for the rest. Equal weight per feature is not equal weight per idea, either: water and sewer coverage are strongly correlated (r = 0.77 over the kept rows), so what they share counts twice. If water safety should weigh more, that is a decision to make explicitly and report, not to leave to the units the data happened to come in.

title: 11  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means
text:
11.1 k-means in four steps
The water data now have 11,235 prepared rows, each described by nine z-scores. Nobody can read that many rows. Clustering turns them into a few kinds that a person can name, compare and act on: these municipal zones are like each other, and unlike those. An official can ask which kinds need which help; a council can see which kind its own zones belong to. Clustering needs no labels, so it is a first look at data nobody has categorised, and an odd cluster can point to a data error or a special case. What it cannot do is explain: clusters describe, they do not show causes.
If the mathematics sounds daunting, it need not be. The algorithm is simple enough to watch step by step, and the judgement it needs, how many kinds to look for, is a decision you can write down and check before seeing the answer.
k-means needs one number up front: \(k\), how many clusters to find. It makes one start, then repeats two moves until they change nothing:
Neither move ever raises the inertia, the sum of squared distances from each point to its centre,
\[\text{inertia} = \sum_{i} \lVert x_i - c_{\ell(i)} \rVert^2 ,\]
where \(c_{\ell(i)}\) is the centre point \(i\) is assigned to, and there are only finitely many ways to group the points, so the algorithm always stops. It does not always stop at the best answer: a bad start can trap it in a worse grouping. Figure 11.1 shows the algorithm on 560 synthetic points in three groups, which are toy data made up for the illustration, not the water data.
Figure 11.2: The same algorithm on the toy points, flattened to two of their three dimensions: the random start, the first assignment, an assignment halfway, and the stable result.
Different starts can end in different groupings, so the real analysis runs k-means from 20 starts (scikit-learn’s n_init) and keeps the one with the lowest inertia. Its starts are not dropped at random, as in the toy. scikit-learn’s default, k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007), picks the first centre at random from the data and each next one with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centre already chosen, which spreads them out and makes a stuck start less likely; scikit-learn uses a greedy variant that draws several candidates at each step and keeps the best. A fixed random seed makes the result the same on every render.

title: 11  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means
text:
11.2 Choosing k
k is a hyperparameter: a setting the algorithm cannot learn from its own objective, since inertia always falls as k grows. The analysis fits k-means for k from 2 to 8 and reads two measures (Figure 11.3). Inertia always falls as k grows, so the question is where it stops falling much, the elbow. The silhouette scores, from −1 to 1, how much closer each point is to its own cluster than to the next one, on a fixed sample of 5,000 rows.








Figure 11.3: Choosing k: inertia (left) and silhouette (right) for k = 2 to 8, fitted on all kept rows. The chosen k is marked.





The rule, written into choose_k() in the analysis script, has three parts:

k = 2 is excluded. Two clusters mostly split urban from rural rows (their adjusted Rand index with the zone is 0.50, where 1 would mean identical), which we knew already.
The elbow: take the smallest k from 3 up after which one more cluster cuts inertia by less than 10%. Here that is k = 4: a fifth cluster cuts inertia by only 7%.
The silhouette check: k’s silhouette must be within 0.01 of the best for k ≥ 3. At k = 4 it is 0.195. The check rules out only k = 8 here.

The elbow is marginal. The fourth cluster itself cuts inertia by 10.8%, only just above the 10% threshold, so a threshold of 11% would pick k = 3 instead.
Two more checks follow the fit. Stability: refits from 5 other seeds agree, with an adjusted Rand index of at least 0.998, so the result does not depend on the start. That says nothing about other data, features or k; a bootstrap or leave-one-year-out refit would test that. Ordering: clusters are numbered by their centre’s IRCA, from lowest to highest, so a re-run keeps the same numbers and colours.






WarningCommon pitfall



A silhouette near 0.2 is low. In the subjective reading Rousseeuw and colleagues propose, a best average silhouette of 0.25 or less means that “no substantial structure has been found” (Struyf, Hubert and Rousseeuw, 1997, Table 2), and the best here, at any k, is 0.24. The kinds overlap: they summarise a continuum rather than separate islands of data. So treat k as a judgement call, and do not force a number of clusters to make a nicer story. Writing the rule down before seeing the result is what keeps such a choice honest; choose_k() at least makes the rule explicit, so anyone can check it and see how close the call was.

title: 11  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means
text:
Summary
Clustering turns thousands of rows into a few kinds that people can name and compare, but it describes and does not explain. k-means makes one start, then repeats two moves, assign each point to its nearest centre and move each centre to its points’ mean, until nothing changes; it never raises inertia but can stall in a worse grouping, so the analysis uses 20 starts and a fixed seed. k is chosen by a written rule: k = 2 is excluded as the urban-rural split, the elbow picks k = 4 by a narrow margin, and the silhouette, 0.19, says the kinds overlap. Refits from other seeds agree, so the result does not depend on the start, though that does not test other data, features or k. PCA gives a picture, not the model; a third component and a relief map show that altitude, one of the features, separates two of the kinds, clusters 2 and 3. Using the finished model is a legitimate route, provided you can explain what it chose. The kinds so far are only numbers, from cluster 1, lowest centre IRCA, to cluster 4: the next chapter works out what sets each one apart, names it by a rule, and compares the outcomes the clustering never saw.

title: 12  Interpreting Clusters
text:
12.1 What sets each cluster apart
Cluster 4 is a number, and a number is hard to act on. “Rural, low-coverage, high-risk water” is a phrase an official can repeat and a council can argue over, and anyone can check it, provided a rule produced it rather than someone’s eye. Names like that come first, for every cluster, with the one Tunja’s zones fall in. Then comes the comparison the analysis was built for: infant mortality, exam scores and school dropout, which the clustering never saw, kind by kind.
That comparison is where readers draw conclusions, so it is where honesty matters most. It gets three views, as medians over time, in standard-deviation units and as full distributions, because each hides something the others show.
A cluster’s profile is the mean of each feature over its rows, in z units: +1 means one standard deviation above that year’s average across all kept rows (Figure 12.1). Read across a row to describe a cluster, and down a column to see which feature separates them.
Figure 12.1: Cluster profiles in z units: standard deviations above (red) or below (blue) the year’s average. IRCA: utility-supplied. Altitude: derived SRTM point.
The highest-IRCA cluster, cluster 4, stands out most on piped-water coverage (−1.3 SD) and sewer coverage (−1.3 SD): a combination of high-risk utility-supplied water, poverty and low coverage, not any one of them. Each cluster is a combination, which is exactly what a single variable could not have found.

title: 12  Interpreting Clusters
text:
12.3 Where Tunja lands
The cluster that holds all 16 of Tunja’s zone-years, urban and rural, now has a name: cluster 1 (cities and large towns), “Cities and large towns, no-risk water”. For the urban zone, it fits. For the rural zone, the label hides most of what Section 9.3 found. Its water scored in the high-risk band every year from 2010 to 2014, before the analysis’s window opens in 2016, and inside the window its utility-supplied IRCA is never in the no-risk band, and is in the medium band in three of the eight years.
Two things are at work. The risk word describes the cluster’s median, not each member, as Section 12.2 warned. And k-means places a row by all nine features at once. On its own four, IRCA, piped-water coverage, sewer coverage and poverty, Tunja’s rural zone sits nearest the centre of cluster 4 (rural), and two of those, the coverages, are fills (Section 10.2). On the five it shares with the urban zone as one municipality, rural share, altitude, rainfall, municipal performance and water transfers, it sits nearest cluster 1’s, and those decide. It has company: 33% of that cluster’s zone-years are rural zones. A label describes a kind; to say anything about one member, go back to its rows.

title: 12  Interpreting Clusters
text:
12.4 Outcomes by cluster
Now the outcomes, which the clustering never used (Figure 12.2). Each line is a cluster’s median within each year, so the comparison never mixes years.








Figure 12.2: Median outcome by cluster and year. Infant mortality: 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 only (its method changes in 2017, and 2020 looks like another source). Saber 11: published years. Descriptive only: not causal effects of water safety.





Gaps in the lines are years with no comparable value, drawn as gaps rather than joined across. Infant mortality and dropout are measured for a whole municipality but repeated on both zone rows, so they are counted once per municipality in each cluster and year; Saber 11 is per zone.
Figure 12.3 puts the outcomes on the features’ scale: each outcome standardised within its year, a cell being the cluster’s mean z, with the mean itself in brackets.








Figure 12.3: Cluster mean outcome in z units, on the same colour scale as the features’ heatmap, with the mean itself in brackets. Descriptive only.





The paleness is the finding. No cluster’s mean outcome is more than 0.65 standard deviations from the average, against 1.32 for the features that formed them: the kinds differ less in outcomes than in what defines them. Part of this is by design: k-means chose the clusters to separate the features, so they should differ more on those than on anything else. Within that: the lowest recorded infant mortality is in cluster 1 (cities and large towns) and the highest in cluster 2 (highland towns); the best Saber 11 scores are in cluster 1 (cities and large towns); and the lowest dropout is in cluster 2 (highland towns).






WarningCommon pitfall



The highest recorded infant mortality is not in the cluster with the worst water, cluster 4 (rural). That is a good moment to slow down rather than to explain it away. The rates of cluster 2 (highland towns) come from the smallest places of any kind, a median of 10,680 people per municipality-year, where a handful of deaths moves a rate a long way. And they are only the rates that exist. The series holds no zeros, so from 2017 a blank may be a recorded zero, and 50% of this kind’s municipality-years are blank, against 32% of all clustered municipality-years. Leaving blanks out drops what may be zeros and raises small places’ averages most: a selection on the outcome that may account for part of this kind’s place at the top. Small numbers, reporting and many other differences between the kinds all sit between a cluster’s water and its outcomes. Chapter 13 takes that up directly.

title: 13  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
13.1 Worse water, more infant deaths?
The analysis was built to ask whether places with worse water have worse outcomes, and the temptation, once there is a chart, is to read the answer as an effect: worse water causes more infant deaths. The data cannot support that sentence, and this chapter shows why, with the analysis’s own numbers.
One more comparison, the association between water safety and infant mortality within each kind of place, comes out weak in every kind, and in one as large as across all of them. But neither a strong association nor a weak one could settle the causal question here, and the reasons decide how the results must be written. That last part is not a formality: the sentence a reader quotes is the one you publish.
Across all municipality-years with both values in 2017–2019 and 2021–2023, the rank correlation between utility-supplied IRCA and infant mortality is +0.10 (n = 4,016). Spearman’s \(\rho\) (rho) measures whether two variables rise and fall together in rank order, from −1 (perfectly opposite) through 0 (no monotonic relation) to +1 (perfectly together), and it is not thrown by extreme values, which matters with small municipalities’ noisy rates.
A small positive association across all places could come from water, or from everything that differs between places with safe and unsafe water. The clusters offer a partial control: within a cluster, places are more alike in poverty, rurality, coverage and altitude than across the country, though far from equal (the silhouette in Section 11.2 was 0.19). So the check repeats the comparison inside each cluster (Figure 13.1).
Figure 13.1: Median infant mortality by utility-supplied IRCA band, within each cluster; 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 pooled. Bands with fewer than 20 municipality-years are not drawn. Descriptive only: not a causal effect of water safety.
Within the clusters, \(\rho\) runs from −0.04 in cluster 1 to +0.10 in cluster 2, where it is as large as across all places. Two things make these figures hard to set beside the pooled one. The clusters were formed partly on IRCA, so inside clusters 1 and 2 it varies less: standard deviations of 8.5 and 11.9 against 20.1 across all places, and a narrower range weakens a rank correlation by construction. (In clusters 3 and 4 it varies more, 22.9 and 31.1, and \(\rho\) is weaker there too.) And the units differ, because the unit follows the outcome. Infant mortality is measured for a whole municipality, so each municipality-year counts once, with the mean IRCA of its zones: all of them for the pooled figure, only those in the cluster for a cluster’s.
That mean is unweighted, and it covers only the zones with a score: in 54% of the pooled municipality-years only one zone has one. So the IRCA beside a rate is one zone’s score or the plain mean of two, not what the average resident drinks.
It would be easy to read this as “water does not matter”. That reading is as unsupported as the first one.

title: 13  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
13.2 What else could explain it
Figure 13.2 draws the paths between water and infant mortality that the data cannot separate.






Figure 13.2: What else could explain it. The dashed arrow is the question; every other path can create an association without an effect, or hide an effect that exists.



Poverty and rurality are likely confounders: poorer, more rural places tend to have less safe water and, for other reasons, more infant deaths. They can produce an association between water and mortality with no effect of water at all. Health-service access, worse in poor and remote places, lies on another path to infant deaths. Reporting quality works the other way: places with weak birth and death registration record fewer infant deaths than occur, and if those are also the places with unsafe water, under-recording can hide a real effect. Blanks add a second problem. The series holds no zeros, so a blank rate may mean no deaths were recorded, and 32% of the clustered municipality-years in these years are blank. Leaving them out drops what may be recorded zeros, which raises small places’ averages most: a selection on the outcome itself.
Then there is the ecological level. IRCA is measured for an urban or rural zone, infant mortality for the whole municipality. A pattern across places need not hold for the people in them: the infants who died need not be the ones drinking the worst water. Drawing individual conclusions from aggregate data is known as the ecological fallacy.
Tunja shows the mismatch in one place. In this check each of its six municipality-years counts once in cluster 1, with the mean IRCA of its two zones: in 2018, for example, 9.15, halfway between its urban water’s 0.5 and its rural water’s 17.8, a value neither zone had. The mean weighs the two zones equally, though at most 5% of Tunja’s people live in the rural one, and the infant mortality beside it is the whole municipality’s.
The clusters narrow some of these differences without removing them: within a cluster, places still differ in poverty and access. And small municipalities produce extreme rates, which add noise that flattens any line.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. Pick one of these. Could it hide a real effect, or create a fake one?
Poverty can create a fake one: if poorer places tend to have both less safe water and, for other reasons, more infant deaths, the two move together without water doing anything. Reporting quality can hide a real one: if unsafe-water places under-record deaths, their measured rates are too low, and a real effect looks smaller than it is. Most confounders can push either way, which is exactly why a correlation cannot settle the question.


A causal claim needs a design that handles these paths, not a better chart: for example, comparing places before and after a change in water treatment, against comparable places without the change. That is a different study, with different data.

13.3 Writing it honestly
Every output of this analysis says the same thing in the same words, because the project’s rules require it: comparisons between clusters are descriptive and do not establish a causal effect of water safety. In practice that means a few habits:

Describe what was compared, and over which rows: “within each cluster, 2017–2019 and 2021–2023, municipality-years with both values”.
Use verbs of association (“is higher in”, “varies with”), not of effect (“raises”, “reduces”, “leads to”).
Name the data’s limits beside the result: the utility-supplied IRCA, the method change in infant mortality, the zone-versus-municipality mismatch.
State what the result does not show, in one sentence a reader could quote.







WarningCommon pitfall



The causal sentence usually arrives in the last step: a slide title, a blog post’s headline, a summary for a council. Ask the assistant to check every title and summary against the project’s rules, and read them yourself. “Utility-supplied water risk (IRCA) and infant mortality in Colombian municipalities” is a fair title; “How unsafe water kills infants” is not, however strongly you suspect it.

title: 14  Publish Many
text:
14.1 The report, in Word and PDF
The officials will read the findings as a report, so they need it in the formats offices pass around: Word and PDF. The municipal council will see them on a screen in a meeting, and will look to the last slide for the conclusion. Both will look for where to act, and anyone else needs a link. So the project gets a report, slides, and a website with a blog post, and not one of them may compute anything. Each reads outputs/, and that is what makes the chapter’s last test fair: change one setting in the analysis, predict what follows, rebuild, and check that every publication followed. On the way, the old trade-off between recomputing and caching comes back, now that the project is big enough for it to matter.

The publications become one website, with a blog post that tells the story in prose:
# _quarto.yml
project:
  type: website
1  execute-dir: project
2  pre-render: scripts/analysis.py
execute:
3  freeze: false

1

2

Quarto runs the analysis before every render, including a single page’s render: outputs/ is always fresh.

3

Every render re-executes every page, so every page shows the outputs just written.


# index.qmd
listing:
1  contents: posts

1

You do

The finished post protects itself with one line in its setup cell, assert k == 4, which fails the render if the analysis ever finds a different k. A loud failure is better than a quiet falsehood (Figure 14.3).






Figure 14.3: The finished blog post, whose title states the number of clusters the analysis found. Rendered from examples/water/posts/four-kinds-of-municipal-zone/index.qmd.




14.4.1 Fresh or frozen?
freeze: false is the simple, safe setting: every render recomputes everything, so nothing can be stale. The cost is time, every render, for every page. freeze: auto is the alternative: Quarto stores each page’s results in _freeze/ and re-executes a page only when its own source changes.
The catch is in that last phrase. Quarto does not know which files a page reads, so a change to data/ or to outputs/ is not detected, and a frozen page keeps its old numbers. With freeze: auto you need a rule for throwing results away: delete _freeze/ (or render that one page directly, which ignores the cache) whenever the data or the analysis change.






TipIn practice



Start with freeze: false and switch only when renders become slow enough to matter, and when you do, write the invalidation rule down where the next person will find it. This book uses freeze: auto, so the EPUB rebuilds quickly and reproducibly, and its rule is written in its configuration and README: after any change to the examples’ data or analysis, run make book-fresh, which deletes _freeze/ and re-executes every chapter.

Figure 14.4: The finished dashboard’s map page. Rendered from examples/water/dashboard.qmd.









WarningCommon pitfall



Three traps, all met building the example. The boundary file follows the GeoJSON standard (exterior rings counter-clockwise) and Plotly expects the opposite, so without reversing the rings every municipality is drawn as “the world minus the municipality”, a grey rectangle; the finished script’s load_geojson() reverses them. Animation frames must update only the colours (z): if every year repeats the 2.7 MB of boundaries, the page balloons. And a dashboard cell shows every top-level expression, not only the last, so a bare fig.add_vline(…) draws the chart twice; assign it, fig = fig.add_vline(…), and end the cell with fig. The searchable table needs maxBytes=0, or itables silently drops rows to keep the page small.


The same outputs can also become an academic paper, as London’s did (Section 7.6), now with numbered equations ($$ … $$ {#eq-kmeans}, referred to as @eq-kmeans) and citations of the papers behind each method:



Ask your coding assistant

Create whitepaper.qmd from outputs/: A4 Typst, "New Computer Modern"; an abstract (no inline code), numbered Introduction, Methods with equations, Results and Conclusions, then References via `#set bibliography(title: [References])`. Cite data/README.md's sources and the k-means, silhouette and ARI papers in references.bib; open each DOI. Add it to `render` and the "Downloads" menu; render; check equations and citations. Figures must be vector: set `fig-format: svg` and check that the files in `figure-typst/` end in .svg.








WarningCommon pitfall



“Open each DOI” is there for a reason: an assistant can produce a plausible reference that does not exist. Ask it to drop any reference it cannot open rather than guess, and check the reference list yourself. The finished paper cites Lloyd (1982) for k-means, Rousseeuw (1987) for the silhouette, Hubert and Arabie (1985) for the adjusted Rand index and Pedregosa et al. (2011) for scikit-learn, each checked against its publisher’s page on 2026-11-01.

14.8 Further challenges
These have no checkpoints. Each extends the analysis with data already in the project, or names one that is not yet available:

Moves between kinds. Count how municipalities’ zones move between clusters from 2016 to 2023, and draw it as a Sankey diagram (Plotly’s go.Sankey).
Positive deviants. Find municipalities whose rural zone is in the high-risk kind yet whose recorded infant mortality is low, and check first whether that is small numbers, blanks or under-registration.
Other clusterings. A Gaussian mixture model gives each row a probability per cluster instead of a hard label; HDBSCAN finds dense groups and leaves outliers unclustered. Do the kinds survive?
A better outcome. Diarrhoeal disease in children under five is the outcome most directly linked to water. Its incidence is not in the open SIVIGILA data, which publish only deaths; the data’s README records it as a source to add when it becomes available.

title: 14  Publish Many
text:
Summary
Part III ends on a prediction. Set MAX_MISSING to 1, and every row missing more than one of the nine features goes. Department capitals have no zone-level coverage, so their rural zones reach that rule with both coverage values missing (imputation comes after the rule): predict that every one of their rural zone-years will go, Tunja’s eight among them, along with every other zone-year missing both coverages, while Tunja’s urban zone, which takes the municipal total, stays. Then rebuild, and check. pre-render re-runs the analysis and freeze: false re-executes every page. The kept rows fall from 11,235 to 10,583: the capitals’ 135 rural zone-years and 517 other zone-years missing both coverages, and nothing else; Tunja’s urban zone stays in cluster 1 in every year. k stays 4, so the post’s assert k == 4 passes, the names stay, and 98% of the remaining rows keep their cluster. The officials’ report, the council’s slides, the post and the dashboard all change together, because none of them computes anything; the live site does not change at all until you publish again.
That one exercise holds the part’s design: one script, every publication reading its outputs/, pre-render and freeze: false keeping both fresh (freeze: auto is faster, but needs a written rule for clearing its cache), and guards that turn a silent inconsistency into a failed render. It is also the book’s method at full size, and the afterword takes it back to its three verbs, and to a project of your own.

text:
Answers to the review questions

Because the analysis then compares outcomes between the kinds. If infant mortality helped define them, they would differ in infant mortality by construction, and the comparison would find exactly what was put in (Features and outcomes). Outcomes describe the clusters; they never define them.
The open table holds the IRCA of systems run by water utilities, not the national figure. Self-supplied systems, which have no utility, score far worse (Scoring water risk: the IRCA), so the data understate the risk wherever people rely on self-supply, and say nothing where no utility exists. Without the label, a reader would take the figure for the national one, and think water safer than it is wherever self-supply is common.
Right about the kind, wrong about this member: Tunja’s rural water was never in the no-risk band in 2016–2023. The risk word is the band of the cluster’s median IRCA, not a claim about every zone-year in it, and k-means places a row by all nine features, several of which Tunja’s two zones share as one municipality (Name them by a rule, Where Tunja lands). A statement about Tunja needs Tunja’s rows.
Both read a description as an effect. The first turns a difference between kinds into a cause, though poverty, rurality, health-service access and reporting differ between the kinds too. The second reads a weak association as no effect, though weak reporting can hide deaths and small municipalities add noise (What else could explain it). Instead, say what was compared over which rows, with verbs of association, and add one sentence saying the comparison does not establish a causal effect of water safety (Writing it honestly).
pre-render re-runs the analysis, which rewrites outputs/, and freeze: false re-executes every page that reads them, so your folder is fresh. The live site is the last _site/ you published, and changes only when you publish again (Publish it). With freeze: auto, Quarto would re-execute a page only when its own source changed: it does not see outputs/ or data/, so pages would keep their old numbers until the cache was cleared (A website with a blog).

title: Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next
text:
Your own project, in three turns
Near the end of Part III, one setting changed in one script, and the officials’ report, the council’s slides, the blog post and the dashboard all changed with it, without a number retyped. That moment is what the two projects were for. The London guide and the water analysis each started from plain text and data, became a shelf of documents for different readers, and rebuild with one command. The projects will date. The method will not, and it fits on a card.
The order matters more than the tools.
The second format is where the approach starts to repay the setup; the first change to the data is where it pays for itself.
Assistants, models and Quarto’s options will keep changing, and some details in this book with them. The loop does not. Prompt for one thing. Check it against the data. Publish only what you checked, from one source, as often as the data change.

title: Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next
text:
One output, for one reader. Start with the document your readers already ask for, usually a report, in a project folder with its data, kept unchanged, and an AGENTS.md. Prompt for the skeleton; check that it renders and answers the reader’s question.
Make it compute. Replace every typed number with inline code that reads the data, or the results of one analysis script, and guard any sentence whose conclusion depends on them. Check by changing one input in a copy and watching the number move.
Add formats, then readers. Word or a PDF, then slides, then a website, each reading the same results. Check with a prediction: change a setting, say what will change, rebuild and compare. Then publish.

Before you start
This appendix is step 1 of the setup (Section 3.2) for Windows. The workshop’s tools are made for Linux, so on Windows you install Ubuntu, a widely used version of Linux, inside Windows with WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux. Think of Windows as your house, with your browser, files and apps, and Ubuntu as a room inside it, a window where you type commands. Everything in this book happens in that room, your Windows browser still opens what you make, and nothing on Windows is removed.
Why not PowerShell, Windows’s own command window? Because the book’s commands, and the way the setup was tested, are for Linux. Some tools have Windows installers, but their paths and commands differ, and each variant is another way to go wrong.
Figure A.1 shows the whole procedure in one window. The steps below go slowly, with a restart in the middle, and the first time Ubuntu opens it also asks you to choose a username and password, which the animation skips.
Do one step, compare your screen with You should see, then go on. If something looks different, see If you are stuck.

title: Appendix B — Terminal Keys and Habits

Know where you are. Run pwd before starting an assistant: its answer is the assistant’s root folder (Section 2.4).
Two tabs. Keep the assistant in one tab and commands such as quarto preview in another, both in the project folder.
New tab after installing. A terminal learns where programs are when it starts, so a program installed a moment ago is “not found” until you open a new tab.
Read before you run. Whether a command comes from the book, a web chat or the assistant, read it before you press Enter or approve it, especially anything with sudo or rm.
Copy errors whole. When something fails, copy the command and the entire error text; the useful line is rarely the last one.

title: Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers
text:
Answer: changing a London input
The task (Section 7.5): set the Tower of London’s visits_2025 to 8,000,000.
What changes. Every page that loads attractions.csv (Table 7.1) is rebuilt with the new count, and what it shows depends on its code. The guide, in every format it writes (web page, Word and PDF, and PowerPoint, slides and EPUB if made), the dashboard’s value boxes and bar chart, and the partner brief (london-email.docx) find the top attraction with idxmax() and the total with .sum(), so the Tower of London becomes the most visited attraction and the total rises. The square advert, if made, uses only idxmax(), so it names the Tower too. The white paper names no top attraction: its sums by admission change, but its table keeps ALVA’s rank_uk column from the file, so it would still rank the Tower ninth in the UK beside the most visits of the ten. A copied column goes stale too.
What does not. The flyer, which copies its facts and quotes no visit counts; the covering email (london-email-message.md), which quotes no numbers and is not rendered; the dashboard’s line chart and the 3-D map, which read visits.csv, not attractions.csv; any output not rebuilt; and the live site, until it is published again.
Why. Every render re-runs every page’s code (freeze: false), and each changed output is linked to the input by a line of code that loads it. A strong answer names that line.
Follow-up questions worth asking. Where would the change appear if the number had been typed into the prose instead of computed? (Nowhere: the typed number would silently disagree with the chart.) What would change if visits.csv were edited instead? (The dashboard’s line chart, the 3-D map and the white paper’s trend.) Why does the render re-run every cell? (Because nothing is cached; see Section 14.4.)

The stricter setting drops 652 more rows, those missing exactly two features. 652 of them are missing both coverage values: zones whose urban and rural coverage split is missing that year. 142 belong to department capitals, mostly their rural zones (the urban ones take the municipal total). k stays 4, so the blog post’s assert k == 4 still passes; a setting that changed k would make the post fail its render, by design.
What changes. pre-render re-runs scripts/analysis.py, which rewrites every file in outputs/ (clusters.parquet, cluster_profiles.csv, k_selection.csv, stability.csv, outcomes_by_year.csv, irca_infant.csv, irca_infant_bins.csv and summary.json), and freeze: false re-executes every page, so the explore and clusters pages, the report in every format, the slides, the blog post and the dashboard all change together.
What does not. data/, the page sources, the post’s title (k is still 4) and, until it is published again, the live site.
Why. Compute once, publish many: one setting in one script, read by every publication. Strong answers name the mechanism (pre-render, outputs/, freeze: false) and check at least two outputs against the new row counts. Undo with git restore scripts/analysis.py.

text:
The book is written in English, but its tools need not be used in English.
The website edition can be translated by your browser. In Chrome, the Google Translate extension translates the page in place (checked 2026-10-30). Code stays as written: translators skip code, so commands, file names and the prompts in the assistant boxes remain in English. That is deliberate. The prompts name files, columns and options that must match your project exactly, and a translated file name would no longer be found.
The assistant understands many languages. You can write your own prompts in Spanish, or any other language the model knows, and keep the literal names in backticks so they are not translated. To have the assistant answer in Spanish while leaving code alone, make your first prompt:



Ask your coding assistant

Responde siempre en español; deja el código y los nombres de archivo en inglés.


(“Always reply in Spanish; leave code and file names in English.”)
The workshop’s slides, which this book follows, were designed for browser translation: their prompts are translated for reading, while file names, columns and options are marked to stay in English.






TipIn practice



A translated page can mistranslate technical words. In testing, Google Translate rendered the column name mdm as “señora” and “Render” as “Prestar”. When a translated sentence seems odd, check the original, and always copy literal names from the code, never from translated prose.

title: Appendix H — How This Book Is Built
text:
One source, two editions
This book is a Quarto book project in the book/ folder of the workshop repository, built into two editions from one set of chapter files: an EPUB e-book and a website. It is a worked example of the book’s own subject, and its problems are worth recording, because most of them were invisible until the EPUB was checked on a phone screen or by a validator.
The chapters are .qmd files. Their Python cells compute every number from the repository’s data, by reading the London files and by importing the water project’s analysis.py, so the book quotes exactly what the projects compute. Results are cached with freeze: auto, so the EPUB rebuilds quickly and the same way each time; the rule for clearing the cache, written in the configuration and the README, is to run make book-fresh after any change to the examples’ data or analysis.
Content meant for one edition is marked for it. Live 3-D scenes and data explorers are wrapped in ::: {.content-visible when-format="html:js"}, and their EPUB stand-ins, animations with a link and a QR code, in when-format="epub". The HTML edition runs the workshop’s own three.js bundle, unchanged, through a small script that imitates the slide framework the bundle expects.

Table H.1: Problems met building the EPUB edition, and their fixes.









Problem
Fix




Quarto 1.10.20 drops a book’s parts, and the part pages’ content, from the EPUB
Part pages are ordinary chapters in the EPUB; a post-render script nests each part’s chapters under it in the table of contents


A profile’s chapter list is added to the base list, not substituted for it
One master list (_chapters.yml) generates a chapter list for each edition


when-format="html" also matches EPUB
HTML-only content uses when-format="html:js"


Rendering one edition empties the other’s output folder
Each edition has its own output folder


Quarto’s figure wrapper carries an alt attribute that EPUB’s XHTML forbids
The post-render script removes it (the image keeps its alt text)


No landmarks for the copyright page or the start of the text
Added by the post-render script, which also puts the copyright page before the preface


Callout titles and code have fixed light backgrounds and dark text, invisible in a reader’s night theme
The stylesheet lets the reader’s colours through


Code lines do not wrap on a phone, and cell outputs scroll sideways
The stylesheet makes long lines wrap and outputs fit


Wide diagrams are unreadable on a phone
Diagrams are drawn portrait, 700 pixels wide with text of at least 19 pixels, and supplied as PNG at double resolution






The finished EPUB passes EPUBCheck 5.4.0, the W3C’s validator, with no errors and no warnings.

Before the day

Collect test-run confirmations. Ask every participant to confirm the setup check and the test run (Section 3.7), and contact anyone who has not.
Windows. Ask for wsl -l -v output showing VERSION 2 before the day. Participants without an administrator account, or with virtualisation off in the BIOS, cannot install WSL: pair them with a neighbour. The Windows procedure has been checked against Microsoft’s documentation and on a Mac; run it once on a clean Windows machine before teaching.
The network. Check that the venue’s Wi-Fi allows GitHub, uv’s package downloads and GitHub Pages, and copes with everyone downloading at once.

title: Appendix I — Running This as a Workshop
text:
The two-minute rule
The rule that keeps the room together: anyone stuck for two minutes on a command, an assistant error or a typo does not debug in front of the room. They paste the exercise’s catch-up line (Figure 1), and everyone is hands-on together again at the next block. Demonstrate the catch-up once, live, early in the first block, so that nobody treats it as failing. In the 0:15 block, a helper sits with anyone whose setup check or test run failed while the presenter carries on.
From the Cluster block on, keep the room on the normal route, which copies each block’s finished analysis.py. The challenge route, writing the analysis, is for people well ahead of the room; agenda times assume the normal route.

text:
Publishing
The first publish of each site takes about two minutes from creating the gh-pages branch to pushing the site, and GitHub Pages then builds it in 20 to 35 seconds (dry run, 2026-11-01). Use the wait: show one of the finished example sites, or explain how the gh-pages branch works. The three commonest problems are the first publish (it must be interactive), a push failing with HTTP 400 (raise http.postBuffer), and a render colliding with a running preview (stop the preview first); Appendix D has the fixes.
